S01.asr: You've saved 10 % of a home's price. Do you buy now and pay mortgage insurance or keep renting until you reach 20 %?

S02.asr: On the schedule alone, you can't even ask to cancel it for about 8 years. We replayed real U .S. prices and rates month by month, so you'll see how long it took on paper, typically and in slow cases.

S04.asr: Private Mortgage Insurance, or PMI, is a policy lenders usually require on a conventional loan with less than 20 % down. It protects the loan goes bad, but the borrower pays for it, month after month, on top of the mortgage. What it costs depends on the loan and the borrower, so this video puts no dollar figure on it. What we can measure is how long it lasts. So when does it end?

S05.asr: Here's an illustrative example. A $400 ,000 home, a little under the national median price of new homes sold from April through June. With 10 % down, that leaves a $360 ,000 loan.

S06.asr: At September's average mortgage rate, 6 .86%, the monthly payment for principal and interest is the figure on screen. Taxes, home insurance, and the mortgage insurance all come on top of it. Each payment pays the balance down a little, slowly at first, and faster later on.

S07.asr: By federal law, the borrower can ask to cancel the insurance once the schedule says the loan is down to 80 % of the original value, here, $320 ,000. On this loan, that's payment 99, the date this video opened with. That request comes with conditions, such as being current on payments.

S08.asr: And the insurance has to end automatically when the schedule reaches 78 percent, as long as payments are current. Here, that's about 9 .5 years in. Both dates come from the schedule alone, and both ignore what the house is worth.

S09.asr: Lenders and the investors who own loans can also drop the insurance based on the home's current value. If prices rise, the same balance becomes a smaller share of the home, and 80 % can arrive sooner on paper. That's what on paper means in this video, and a lender's request, appraisal, and minimum time still come after it. So how fast did rising prices actually get 10 % down buyers there?

S10.asr: We took every purchase month from January 1991 to July 2016. For each one, we set up the same 10 % down loan at that month's average rate. And we let the home's value move exactly like the Federal Housing Finance Agency's National Index of Home Purchase Prices. Every month after that, we compare the balance with the value and stop the clock the first time the loan is 80 % or less. Each bar here is one purchase month, and its height shows how long that took.

S11.asr: The typical answer, 23 months. Half of the purchase months got there sooner, and half took longer. And in 90 .6 % of them, prices got the loan to 80 % on paper no later than the schedule would have. That's the gap between the schedule's long road and the replay's typical one.

S13.asr: The typical case also hides a long tail. About one in seven purchase months took more than five years. They sit together in one stretch of the grid, the months just before and during the national price slump.

S14.asr: The slowest was October 2005, 112 months on paper. That's longer than the schedule itself took at that month's rate. And this is a national average. No single home tracks it, and a local market can do much better or much worse. So why did the same rule give such different answers?

S15.asr: Three illustrative buyers, each with 10 % down, show why. Gray's bought in June 2014 at 4 .16%. Her loan reached 80 % on paper right at the middle of the replay. She is the typical case from before. Her own schedule would have taken several years longer.

S16.asr: Owen bought in January 2004 while prices were climbing fast. He reached 80 % on paper in 13 months, the fastest in the replay. Rising prices did most of that work, not his payments.

S17.asr: Victor bought the year after Owen in October 2005, the slowest month in the replay. Prices rose a little, then fell for years, and even when he finally reached 80 % on paper, the index was still below where it started. He got there by paying the loan down, and his own schedule, at his lower rate of 6 .07%, reached 80 % of the original price first, at payment 90. Whether a lender would have dropped his insurance at that point, this data can't show.

S18.asr: Same rule, same national index. What differed was the month they started and what prices did next. So a plan can be measured against two benchmarks from this history. One is the schedule the law uses, which on the example loan runs most of a decade. The other is history on paper. A plan that counts on about two years matched the typical month, math, not the slow ones, and not the lender's step. On the illustrated $400 ,000 home, the other path, 20 % down, means $40 ,000 more upfront. This video doesn't weigh that against renting or waiting. It measures how long the insurance math took.

S19.asr: How we know this and what this video leaves out is on this card and in the description.

S20.asr: So, how long does the insurance last? On the schedule, the answer is set the day the loan starts. On paper, history gave answers from about a year to more than nine years. And on paper is never the same as removed. This is U .S. only, and it's history, not a forecast.

S03.asr: On paper means the loan is 80 % of the home's value by a national price index. That's not the same as getting the insurance removed. Removal on today's value, when you ask, is the loan owner's rule. For Fannie Mae loans, that's two years and a 75 % bar. You'll also meet three illustrative buyers who got very different answers. It's US only. History, not a forecast. And it won't say whether to buy or wait.

S12.asr: But that's on paper. We also checked a larger set, every purchase month since January 1991, with two years of prices after it. Two years after purchase, only 15 .6 % of them were at or below the 75 % bar Fannie Mae sets for its loans, when a borrower asks to cancel on today's value, a separate route from the law's schedule. So, reaching 80 % on paper in about two years was common in this history, while clearing that early bar by then was not.
